content:
Creating a realistic digital twin for industrial robotics has become essential for modern automation. From testing perception models to validating motion planning pipelines, a high‑fidelity simulation can drastically reduce development time and risk. ⚙️🤖

This article presents a complete industrial digital‑twin workflow built with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, ROS 2, and GPU‑accelerated planning tools. The system tightly integrates physical robots, sensors, and simulated assets to enable accurate comparison, rapid prototyping, and data‑driven robot development.

Overview

The digital twin mirrors a real industrial robot cell containing two 6‑axis manipulators, grippers, RGB and stereo vision sensors, and force‑torque sensing. By synchronizing all physical robot states, camera streams, and controller commands with Isaac Sim, the system becomes a unified playground for:

  • virtual commissioning
  • teleoperation testing
  • perception model validation
  • safe trajectory planning
  • data‑driven behavior development

This setup allows developers to evaluate algorithms in a controlled, reproducible environment—before deploying on expensive hardware.

Hardware Setup

The real-world cell consists of:

  • Robots: UR10 (Universal Robots) and HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman)
  • Grippers: Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85
  • Cameras: Robotiq wrist cameras + Zed 2i stereo cameras
  • Sensors: Robotiq FT300‑S force‑torque sensor
  • Teleoperation: Dual joysticks
  • Compute: Ubuntu PC for Isaac Sim, robot control, and data logging

These components form the foundation for synchronizing physical actions with the simulation environment.

Software Stack

The system runs on a modern robotics toolchain:

  • Ubuntu 22.04 LTS as the OS
  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital‑twin simulation
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and messaging
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation
  • CuRobo + Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated, collision‑free path planning
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for detection and pose estimation
  • Python, C++, Git, Docker for development

This stack ensures real‑time communication, fast trajectory generation, and compatibility across both real and simulated setups.

Building the Digital Twin

1. Data Acquisition

The physical system is assembled, calibrated, and connected to a ROS 2 PC. URDF robot descriptions, camera transformations, and sensor streams (RGB, depth, FT data) are captured and logged. Hand‑eye calibration aligns every sensor with each robot’s TCP to ensure precise reconstruction.

2. Digital Model Creation

URDF models are converted to USD assets for Isaac Sim.
An Extended Robot Description Format (XRDF) is created for CuRobo‑based control inside the simulator. The same planner is then used on real hardware, ensuring matching trajectories in both environments.

3. Teleoperation & Perception Validation

Joystick‑based teleoperation verifies control consistency.
Sensor alignment is tested by comparing real and simulated camera outputs.
Perception models such as YOLO, RF‑DETR, FoundationPose, and DOPE are evaluated to ensure accurate sim‑to‑real transfer.

Results

System Performance Highlights

  • Real robot control via ROS at ~100 Hz
  • Stereo cameras running 1080p @ 30 FPS
  • Isaac Sim simulation operating at ~30 FPS
  • Real‑time collision‑free planning using CuRobo + Nvblox
  • Fully teleoperable dual‑robot setup with simultaneous motion

The digital twin faithfully mirrors robot behavior, enabling safe, repeatable experimentation.

Perception Experiments

A complete synthetic‑data pipeline was built using Isaac Sim:

  • A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and imported as USD.
  • 50,000 synthetic training images were rendered using domain randomization.
  • A DOPE model was trained for 13.74 days on an A100 GPU.
  • Pose‑estimation accuracy was verified in simulation and on a real 3D‑printed object.

This confirms reliable sim‑to‑real transfer, a major requirement for industrial AI workflows.

Conclusion

This digital twin demonstrates how Isaac Sim, ROS 2, and GPU‑accelerated path planning can together form a powerful platform for robotics research and industrial prototyping. The system enables:

  • faster development cycles
  • safer testing
  • reproducible experiments
  • large‑scale synthetic data generation
  • seamless deployment to real robots

The methodology can be applied to other robot platforms and extended for broader industrial use cases.

Future Work

Planned expansions of the digital twin include:

  • OpenPose integration for human‑robot interaction
  • Behavior‑tree‑based control for complex workflows
  • Larger synthetic datasets for improved perception
  • Multi‑robot cooperation and dynamic task allocation
  • Reinforcement learning for adaptive behavior

The vision is a fully scalable, autonomous, and intelligent robotic development environment.
description: A data‑driven digital twin setup that connects real industrial robots with physics‑based simulation for virtual commissioning, perception testing, and advanced robotic development.
title: Building a Digital Twin for Industrial Robotics Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim

abstract: | This paper describes an industrial digital twin setup based on NVIDIA [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} for robotics research and applied development. The system connects real industrial robot hardware with a physics-based simulation environment to enable virtual commissioning, perception testing, and reconfiguration of robotic processes through data-driven insights. The setup implements [CUDA]{acronym-label=“CUDA” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} generated robot trajectories for real-time collision avoidance, has teleoperation control, and can be used to test algorithms for intelligent robotic behaviors in industrial environments.

Keywords: [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, Digital Twin, Robotics, Robot Operating System ([ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}), Collaboration of Industrial Manipulators, Teleoperation. author:

  • | Shivam Shivam^1^, Matthias Hien^1^, Tobias Schaffer^1^
    ^1^Technische Hochschule Deggendorf (THD) bibliography:
  • references.bib title: Digital Twin for Data-Driven Development of Industrial Robots

Introduction

Digital twins allow robotics systems to be developed, tested, and optimized in simulation before or alongside operation on real hardware.[@Malik2024] The presented setup integrates industrial manipulators, grippers, and vision sensors with [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} to create a unified development and experimentation platform. In addition, the framework supports rapid prototyping and iterative testing, enabling us to evaluate control strategies, perception algorithms, and task-level behaviors under consistent and reproducible conditions.

System Overview

The system consists of a physical robotic setup and a corresponding digital model inside [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}. Robot states, sensor data, and control commands are synchronized through [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@doi:10.1126/scirobotics.abm6074], allowing real and simulated executions to be compared and logged.

Hardware Components

Component Description Qty.

Industrial robots 6-axis robotic arms for manipulation tasks; [UR10]{acronym-label=“UR10” acronym-form=“singular+short”} (Universal Robots) and [HC10DT]{acronym-label=“HC10DT” acronym-form=“singular+short”} (Yaskawa Motoman) 2 Grippers Electrically actuated two finger grippers from Robotiq ([2f-140 and 2f-85]{acronym-label=“2f-140 and 2f-85” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}) mounted on [UR10]{acronym-label=“UR10” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} and [HC10DT]{acronym-label=“HC10DT” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} respectively. 2 [RGB]{acronym-label=“RGB” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} Cameras Robotiq [wrist cameras]{acronym-label=“wrist cameras” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} installed on each robot. 2 Force-Torque Sensor Robotiq [FT300-S]{acronym-label=“FT300-S” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} installed on [UR10]{acronym-label=“UR10” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}. 1 Stereo Cameras Stereolabs [Zed 2i]{acronym-label=“Zed 2i” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} mounted on a panel above the robots for perception tasks. 2 Joysticks Controllers for teleoperation of robotic arms. 2 Computation A [PC]{acronym-label=“PC” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} for [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, data processing, and control. 1

: Main hardware components of the digital twin setup.

Software Stack

Layer Software Version

Operating system Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Digital twin NVIDIA [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} 5.0 Robot middleware  [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} 2 Humble Teleoperation  [MoveIt]{acronym-label=“MoveIt” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} Servo 2.5.7 Collision-free path planning  [CuRobo]{acronym-label=“CuRobo” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} with Nvblox 0.7.7 Object detection  [YOLO]{acronym-label=“YOLO” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, RF-DETR [@rf-detr] v8, 3.12.3 Pose estimation  [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1809-10790], FoundationPose [@wen2024foundationposeunified6dpose] – Development tools Python, C++, Bash, Git, Docker –

: Software stack used in the digital twin setup.

Digital Twin Model

The digital twin is implemented using NVIDIA [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} 5.0. Robots, grippers, and the workcell environment are represented as [USD]{acronym-label=“USD” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} assets inside [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}. Kinematic models, camera placement, and collision geometry are aligned with the real setup to ensure that the simulated system closely matches the physical setup.

Methodology

The development workflow of the digital twin setup is organized into three major stages:

  1. Data acquisition from the physical system. In the first stage, the physical setup is assembled and the grippers, cameras are mounted on the robot. The robots, grippers, and cameras are configured and interfaced with the [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [PC]{acronym-label=“PC” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}. Their kinematics and hardware specifications are defined through [URDF]{acronym-label=“URDF” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} files, and additional [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} packages are developed to enable seamless control of all hardware components. Using hand-eye calibration, the transformations (TF) between robots and cameras are calculated. In this way, all sensor streams ([RGB]{acronym-label=“RGB” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, depth, force-torque), robot joint states and gripper feedback get captured and are controllable in [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, thus, forming the basis for accurate digital-twin reconstruction.

  2. Digital Twin Construction and Path Planning The second stage focuses on creating digital assets of the physical setup. The [URDF]{acronym-label=“URDF” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} models of the robot and grippers are converted into [USD]{acronym-label=“USD” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} assets for their integration in Isaac Sim. An Extended Robot Description Format (XRDF) is also designed in order to control the robots in Isaac Sim using [CuRobo]{acronym-label=“CuRobo” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@curobo_report23]. This allowed significantly faster generation of trajectories compared to [OMPL]{acronym-label=“OMPL” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}-based planners in MoveIt, owing to [CuRobo]{acronym-label=“CuRobo” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}’s parallel [GPU]{acronym-label=“GPU” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} computation. The digital twin setup is controllable using [Isaac ROS]{acronym-label=“Isaac ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} with the same naming conventions as in physical robot. The same [CuRobo]{acronym-label=“CuRobo” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@curobo_report23] library is then deployed on the physical setup, ensuring consistent path planning behavior between the virtual and physical systems.

  3. Validation through teleoperation and perception models. Validation is performed by comparing robot trajectories and camera images between the real and simulated environments. The close agreement of motion and sensor alignment confirms that the digital twin is suitable for development and testing tasks. A teleoperation is setup using [MoveIt]{acronym-label=“MoveIt” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} Servo [@moveit] which allows control of robotic arms using joysticks. Object detection and pose estimation models like RF-DETR [@rf-detr], [YOLO]{acronym-label=“YOLO” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@yaseen2024yolov8indepthexplorationinternal] and FoundationPose [@wen2024foundationposeunified6dpose] are tested both in digital twin and real environment for validation. Furthermore, [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} is used to generate training data of [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} model using [SDG]{acronym-label=“SDG” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} and Domain Randomization. The [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} model is then trained and used to estimate object poses in both worlds, verifying accuracy, reliablity and sim-to-real transfer of the digital-twin pipeline.

Results

System Performance

  • The underlying hardware communication of the robot controllers is about 100 Hz with the [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [PC]{acronym-label=“PC” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}.

  • The grippers are communicating via RS485 connection. Both and robots and grippers are controllable with the [ROS]{acronym-label=“ROS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [MoveIt]{acronym-label=“MoveIt” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} library.

  • The stereo cameras operate at 1080p and 30 [FPS]{acronym-label=“FPS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} for generating [RGB]{acronym-label=“RGB” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} and depth maps. This is used to generate voxels using Isaac ROS Nvblox [@millane2024nvbloxgpuacceleratedincrementalsigned] for collision free path planning.

  • The [FT300-S]{acronym-label=“FT300-S” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} sensor and [wrist cameras]{acronym-label=“wrist cameras” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} data stream can be visualized in [RViz]{acronym-label=“RViz” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}.

  • Hand-eye calibration is performed to compute the tranform (TF) between cameras and robot’s [TCP]{acronym-label=“TCP” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, which is then used to place the cameras in the digital twin setup in order to get the same camera data stream but in simulation.

  • The [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} simulation of robots runs at about 30 [FPS]{acronym-label=“FPS” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} with the current [PC]{acronym-label=“PC” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} hardware.

  • Both the robotic arms and grippers are teleoperable via joysticks and the planned trajectories are collision free in real-time, even though the robots are in close proximity of each other.

Perception Results

Object detection models such as [YOLO]{acronym-label=“YOLO” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} [@yaseen2024yolov8indepthexplorationinternal] and RF-DETR [@rf-detr] are tested and evaluated for a sample object using the physical stereo cameras. FoundationPose [@wen2024foundationposeunified6dpose] was also implemented in [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} and physical setup to detect and estimate pose of a sample object.

To further test the capabilities of [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, a [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} model is trained for a custom model called Mustertasse (Figure 2{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img1”}). The object was first designed in CAD and exported as a [USD]{acronym-label=“USD” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} asset for use inside [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}. Using [SDG]{acronym-label=“SDG” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} and domain randomization in [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”}, 50,000 images training dataset for [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} is generated  – 20,000 without any distractor objects and 30,000 with distractor objects. (see Figures 3{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img2”} and 4{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img3”}) The [DOPE]{acronym-label=“DOPE” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} model is then trained on A100 [GPU]{acronym-label=“GPU” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} server for 13.74 days as seen in figure 5{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img4”}. After training, the model was evaluated both in the digital twin and on a physical [FDM]{acronym-label=“FDM” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} 3D-printed part (Figure 6{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img5”} and 7{reference-type=“ref” reference=“fig:img6”}), demonstrating accurate pose estimation and reliable sim-to-real transfer.

All data generated by the digital twin are stored in a structured directory hierarchy that links each experiment to its corresponding simulation scene, robot configuration, and sensor setup. This enables reproducibility, efficient analysis, and long-term dataset management.

Conclusion

The core components are integrated and validated in a laboratory environment. The presented [Isaac Sim]{acronym-label=“Isaac Sim” acronym-form=“singular+abbrv”} digital twin provides a practical and flexible platform for robotics research and industrial prototyping. It enables faster development cycles, reproducible experiments, and data-driven optimization while reducing risk and cost on real hardware. The paper provides a methodology which can be applied for creating realistic digital twins of other robots as well and for the development of robots in general.

Future Works

Future extensions of this digital twin setup will focus on several directions.

  1. Integration of OpenPose library [@8765346] for human-pose estimation to support human-robot interaction scenarios, gesture-based teleoperation, and workspace safety monitoring is to be developed on the setup.

  2. Implementation of a behavior-tree-based control framework is planned to structure complex robotic tasks.

  3. More perception models will be developed using larger synthetic datasets and enhanced domain randomization strategies in Isaac Sim to improve the grasping of objects.

  4. The use of multi-robot coordination and dynamic task allocation will be explored to support more complex industrial workflows. For example, folding of plastic bags.

  5. Reinforcement learning and other data-driven control methods will be implemented to enable adaptive robot behaviors that improve over time.

Creating a realistic digital twin for industrial robotics has become essential for modern automation. From testing perception models to validating motion planning pipelines, a high‑fidelity simulation can drastically reduce development time and risk. ⚙️🤖

This article presents a complete industrial digital‑twin workflow built with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, ROS 2, and GPU‑accelerated planning tools. The system tightly integrates physical robots, sensors, and simulated assets to enable accurate comparison, rapid prototyping, and data‑driven robot development.

Overview

The digital twin mirrors a real industrial robot cell containing two 6‑axis manipulators, grippers, RGB and stereo vision sensors, and force‑torque sensing. By synchronizing all physical robot states, camera streams, and controller commands with Isaac Sim, the system becomes a unified playground for:

  • virtual commissioning
  • teleoperation testing
  • perception model validation
  • safe trajectory planning
  • data‑driven behavior development

This setup allows developers to evaluate algorithms in a controlled, reproducible environment—before deploying on expensive hardware.

Hardware Setup

The real-world cell consists of:

  • Robots: UR10 (Universal Robots) and HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman)
  • Grippers: Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85
  • Cameras: Robotiq wrist cameras + Zed 2i stereo cameras
  • Sensors: Robotiq FT300‑S force‑torque sensor
  • Teleoperation: Dual joysticks
  • Compute: Ubuntu PC for Isaac Sim, robot control, and data logging

These components form the foundation for synchronizing physical actions with the simulation environment.

Software Stack

The system runs on a modern robotics toolchain:

  • Ubuntu 22.04 LTS as the OS
  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital‑twin simulation
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and messaging
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation
  • CuRobo + Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated, collision‑free path planning
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for detection and pose estimation
  • Python, C++, Git, Docker for development

This stack ensures real‑time communication, fast trajectory generation, and compatibility across both real and simulated setups.

Building the Digital Twin

1. Data Acquisition

The physical system is assembled, calibrated, and connected to a ROS 2 PC. URDF robot descriptions, camera transformations, and sensor streams (RGB, depth, FT data) are captured and logged. Hand‑eye calibration aligns every sensor with each robot’s TCP to ensure precise reconstruction.

2. Digital Model Creation

URDF models are converted to USD assets for Isaac Sim.
An Extended Robot Description Format (XRDF) is created for CuRobo‑based control inside the simulator. The same planner is then used on real hardware, ensuring matching trajectories in both environments.

3. Teleoperation & Perception Validation

Joystick‑based teleoperation verifies control consistency.
Sensor alignment is tested by comparing real and simulated camera outputs.
Perception models such as YOLO, RF‑DETR, FoundationPose, and DOPE are evaluated to ensure accurate sim‑to‑real transfer.

Results

System Performance Highlights

  • Real robot control via ROS at ~100 Hz
  • Stereo cameras running 1080p @ 30 FPS
  • Isaac Sim simulation operating at ~30 FPS
  • Real‑time collision‑free planning using CuRobo + Nvblox
  • Fully teleoperable dual‑robot setup with simultaneous motion

The digital twin faithfully mirrors robot behavior, enabling safe, repeatable experimentation.

Perception Experiments

A complete synthetic‑data pipeline was built using Isaac Sim:

  • A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and imported as USD.
  • 50,000 synthetic training images were rendered using domain randomization.
  • A DOPE model was trained for 13.74 days on an A100 GPU.
  • Pose‑estimation accuracy was verified in simulation and on a real 3D‑printed object.

This confirms reliable sim‑to‑real transfer, a major requirement for industrial AI workflows.

Conclusion

This digital twin demonstrates how Isaac Sim, ROS 2, and GPU‑accelerated path planning can together form a powerful platform for robotics research and industrial prototyping. The system enables:

  • faster development cycles
  • safer testing
  • reproducible experiments
  • large‑scale synthetic data generation
  • seamless deployment to real robots

The methodology can be applied to other robot platforms and extended for broader industrial use cases.

Future Work

Planned expansions of the digital twin include:

  • OpenPose integration for human‑robot interaction
  • Behavior‑tree‑based control for complex workflows
  • Larger synthetic datasets for improved perception
  • Multi‑robot cooperation and dynamic task allocation
  • Reinforcement learning for adaptive behavior

The vision is a fully scalable, autonomous, and intelligent robotic development environment.

content:
Abstract

This article presents an industrial digital twin that integrates two 6‑DoF industrial manipulators, grippers, multi‑modal vision, and force‑torque sensing with NVIDIA Isaac Sim via ROS 2. The platform enables virtual commissioning, teleoperation, perception benchmarking, and GPU‑accelerated, collision‑free trajectory generation that is consistent across simulation and physical execution. Empirical results demonstrate real‑time capabilities (∼100 Hz control, 30 FPS stereo perception, and ∼30 FPS simulation), and show reliable sim‑to‑real transfer for object pose estimation using synthetic data generated in Isaac Sim. 1

1. Introduction

Digital twins have become central to modern robotic development by enabling testing, validation, and iteration in a high‑fidelity virtual environment before deployment to physical cells. The setup described here couples real hardware and a physics‑accurate simulation (Isaac Sim 5.0), synchronized through ROS 2, to establish a unified, reproducible platform for algorithm design in manipulation, perception, and task‑level control. 1

2. System Architecture

2.1 Hardware Configuration

The physical cell comprises industrial arms, adaptive grippers, wrist and stereo cameras, and a force‑torque sensor. Teleoperation is enabled via joysticks; an Ubuntu workstation hosts control and simulation. Table 1 summarizes the main components. 1

Table 1 — Main hardware components of the digital‑twin setup

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots 6‑axis manipulators: UR10 (Universal Robots) and HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman) 2
Grippers Electrically actuated Robotiq 2f‑140 (UR10) and 2f‑85 (HC10DT) 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras mounted on each robot 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S installed on UR10 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i pair mounted above the workcell 2
Joysticks Controllers for bilateral teleoperation 2
Computation Ubuntu PC for Isaac Sim, ROS 2 control, data logging 1
1

2.2 Software Stack

The software stack couples simulator, middleware, motion planning, perception, and developer tooling (Table 2). 1

Table 2 — Software stack used in the digital‑twin setup

Layer Software / Library Version / Notes
Operating system Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
Digital twin NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0
Robot middleware ROS 2 Humble
Teleoperation MoveIt Servo 2.5.7
Collision‑free path planning cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox cuRobo; Nvblox 0.7.7
Object detection YOLO; RF‑DETR YOLOv8; RF‑DETR (research)
Pose estimation DOPE; FoundationPose —
Development tools Python, C++, Bash, Git, Docker —
1

3. Digital‑Twin Modeling

Robots, grippers, and the workcell are represented as USD assets in Isaac Sim. Kinematics, collision geometry, and camera extrinsics are aligned with the physical cell through hand‑eye calibration, enabling one‑to‑one comparison of motion and perception across both worlds. A consistent ROS 2 namespace/convention is maintained between simulation and hardware. 1

Figure 1 — Real robotic setup (left) and the corresponding digital twin in Isaac Sim (right).

Rendered from page 2 of the source document. 1

4. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data acquisition. Robots, grippers, and cameras are integrated with ROS 2; URDFs define kinematics and hardware interfaces. RGB, depth, force‑torque streams, joint states, and gripper feedback are synchronized; hand‑eye calibration provides TFs between cameras and TCPs. 1

Stage 2 — Digital‑twin construction and planning. URDFs are converted to USD for Isaac Sim; an Extended Robot Description Format (XRDF) enables cuRobo control inside the simulator. The same GPU‑accelerated planner is deployed on the physical cell, ensuring planner parity between simulation and reality. 1

Stage 3 — Validation via teleoperation and perception. MoveIt Servo provides joystick teleoperation; trajectories and camera frames are compared between sim and real to verify spatiotemporal alignment. Object detection and 6D pose estimation models (YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose) are evaluated in both domains to assess sim‑to‑real reliability. 1

5. Results

5.1 System Performance

  • Robot controllers communicate with the ROS PC at ≈100 Hz. 1
  • Stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS, producing RGB and depth for Isaac ROS Nvblox voxel mapping and collision‑aware planning. 1
  • Isaac Sim runs at ≈30 FPS on the workstation used. 1
  • Both arms and grippers are teleoperable; cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time, collision‑free trajectories even in close‑proximity bimanual configurations. 1

5.2 Perception Experiments and Sim‑to‑Real Transfer

A synthetic‑data pipeline was constructed for a custom Mustertasse object: the CAD model was exported as USD; 50,000 images were generated in Isaac Sim with domain randomization (20k without distractors; 30k with). A DOPE network trained for 13.74 days on an NVIDIA A100 exhibited accurate 6D pose estimation in both simulation and on a physical FDM print of the object. 1

Figure 2 — Data generation and DOPE results for Mustertasse: CAD (a), synthetic datasets (b,c), training curve (d), inference in sim (e) and real (f).

Rendered from page 4 of the source document. 1

6. Discussion

The key advantage of this approach is methodological consistency between virtual and physical execution: identical ROS 2 interfaces, shared naming, and common planners reduce transfer friction and accelerate iteration. GPU‑accelerated planning with cuRobo markedly improves trajectory generation latency relative to CPU‑bound methods, and the integration with Nvblox supplies live signed‑distance fields for safe motion in clutter. The demonstrated perception pipeline underscores the data advantage of simulation (massive, labeled datasets) while validating sim‑to‑real fidelity through controlled physical experiments. 1

7. Future Work

Planned extensions include: (i) integrating OpenPose for HRI and safety monitoring; (ii) a behavior‑tree control architecture for complex tasks; (iii) larger synthetic datasets with richer domain randomization; (iv) multi‑robot coordination and dynamic task allocation; and (v) reinforcement learning for adaptive behaviors. 1

8. Conclusion

The presented digital twin constitutes a practical, laboratory‑validated platform for industrial robotics R&D. By tightly coupling physical hardware with a physics‑based simulator through ROS 2—and by aligning planning, control, and perception across both domains—the system enables reproducible experimentation, rapid prototyping, and data‑driven optimization with reduced risk and cost. 1 ``
description: An academic overview of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital‑twin workflow that couples real hardware with a physics‑based simulation for virtual commissioning, perception evaluation, and GPU‑accelerated motion planning.
title: Digital Twin for Data‑Driven Development of Industrial Robots (Isaac Sim + ROS 2)

content:
Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline. 1

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning. 1

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1
1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.
    1

4. Digital Twin Model

Abstract

This article presents the technical architecture of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline. 1

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning. 1

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1
1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.
    1

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

Figure 1. Real robotic setup (left) and corresponding digital twin (right).

1

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP. 1

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments. 1

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity. 1

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.
    1

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks. 1

content:
Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

Figure 1. Real robotic setup (left) and corresponding digital twin (right).

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

title: Technical Description of an Industrial Digital Twin Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and ROS 2

content:
Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

Figure 1. Real robotic setup (left) and corresponding digital twin (right).

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

content:
Abstract

This article presents the results of a synthetic‑data‑based 6D pose estimation pipeline using Deep Object Pose Estimation (DOPE), trained on Isaac Sim–generated datasets for a custom object (Mustertasse). A 50,000‑image synthetic dataset was created using domain randomization, and the trained model was validated in both simulated and real conditions. The results demonstrate accurate sim‑to‑real transfer, supporting the validity of the digital twin as a perception-test environment. 1

1. Introduction

Reliable 6D pose estimation is essential for robotic manipulation in industrial settings. Synthetic data generated in a digital twin allows scalable training of detection and pose estimation models without costly manual labeling. This study evaluates the DOPE model trained exclusively on Isaac‑Sim‑generated data and assesses its performance across simulated and physical environments. 1

2. Synthetic Data Generation

A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and exported into Isaac Sim as a USD asset. Using Structured Domain Randomization (SDG), 50,000 images were produced:

  • 20,000 images without distractors
  • 30,000 images with distractor objects
    1

Rendered images include diverse object positions, lighting, distractors, and camera noise models, enabling generalization to real-world sensor conditions.

3. DOPE Training

The DOPE network was trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU for 13.74 days, reaching stable convergence by approximately 2,000 epochs. Training was performed exclusively on synthetic Isaac Sim data, which allowed precise 6D labels without manual annotation. 1

4. Results

4.1 DOPE Model Performance

The trained model was evaluated in:

  • Isaac Sim (synthetic validation)
  • Real world using an FDM‑printed Mustertasse replica

Results show high visual alignment between predicted and ground truth poses in both conditions, confirming robust sim‑to‑real transfer. 1

Figure 2 — DOPE Training and Evaluation

CAD model (a), synthetic datasets (b–c), training results (d), inference in simulation (e) and real environment (f).
1

5. Digital Twin Validation via Perception

The DOPE results support the validity of the digital twin because:

  1. Synthetic images produced in Isaac Sim were sufficiently realistic to train a deployable detector.
  2. The model performed consistently on both the simulated object and the real printed counterpart.
  3. Spatial alignment between real and simulated cameras confirmed accurate calibration.
  4. Sim-to-real transfer of detection and pose estimation demonstrates that the twin has correct geometry, lighting models, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics.
    1

6. Discussion

The findings show that combining Isaac Sim with domain randomization enables large-scale, perfectly labeled datasets for industrial object detection. The strong sim‑to‑real consistency further confirms that digital twins can be used to validate machine‑learning‑based robotics workflows before deploying them on hardware. 1

7. Conclusion

The DOPE pipeline trained on digital‑twin‑generated data achieved accurate 6D pose estimation in both simulation and real tests. This validates the digital twin as a perception‑testing platform and highlights synthetic data as a scalable strategy for industrial robotics applications. 1
description: Evaluation of a synthetic-data-driven DOPE pipeline for part detection and pose estimation, and its use in validating a high-fidelity digital twin.
title: Synthetic Data Generation and DOPE-Based Pose Estimation for Industrial Parts Using a Digital Twin

content:
Abstract

This article presents the results of a synthetic‑data‑based 6D pose estimation pipeline using Deep Object Pose Estimation (DOPE), trained on Isaac Sim–generated datasets for a custom object (Mustertasse). A 50,000‑image synthetic dataset was created using domain randomization, and the trained model was validated in both simulated and real conditions. The results demonstrate accurate sim‑to‑real transfer, supporting the validity of the digital twin as a perception-test environment.

1. Introduction

Reliable 6D pose estimation is essential for robotic manipulation in industrial settings. Synthetic data generated in a digital twin allows scalable training of detection and pose estimation models without costly manual labeling. This study evaluates the DOPE model trained exclusively on Isaac‑Sim‑generated data and assesses its performance across simulated and physical environments.

2. Synthetic Data Generation

A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and exported into Isaac Sim as a USD asset. Using Structured Domain Randomization (SDG), 50,000 images were produced:

  • 20,000 images without distractors
  • 30,000 images with distractor objects

Rendered images include diverse object positions, lighting, distractors, and camera noise models, enabling generalization to real-world sensor conditions.

3. DOPE Training

The DOPE network was trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU for 13.74 days, reaching stable convergence by approximately 2,000 epochs. Training was performed exclusively on synthetic Isaac Sim data, which allowed precise 6D labels without manual annotation.

4. Results

4.1 DOPE Model Performance

The trained model was evaluated in:

  • Isaac Sim (synthetic validation)
  • Real world using an FDM‑printed Mustertasse replica

Results show high visual alignment between predicted and ground truth poses in both conditions, confirming robust sim‑to‑real transfer.

Figure 2 — DOPE Training and Evaluation

CAD model (a), synthetic datasets (b–c), training results (d), inference in simulation (e) and real environment (f).

5. Digital Twin Validation via Perception

The DOPE results support the validity of the digital twin because:

  1. Synthetic images produced in Isaac Sim were sufficiently realistic to train a deployable detector.
  2. The model performed consistently on both the simulated object and the real printed counterpart.
  3. Spatial alignment between real and simulated cameras confirmed accurate calibration.
  4. Sim-to-real transfer of detection and pose estimation demonstrates that the twin has correct geometry, lighting models, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics.

6. Discussion

The findings show that combining Isaac Sim with domain randomization enables large-scale, perfectly labeled datasets for industrial object detection. The strong sim‑to‑real consistency further confirms that digital twins can be used to validate machine‑learning‑based robotics workflows before deploying them on hardware.

7. Conclusion

The DOPE pipeline trained on digital‑twin‑generated data achieved accurate 6D pose estimation in both simulation and real tests. This validates the digital twin as a perception‑testing platform and highlights synthetic data as a scalable strategy for industrial robotics applications.

Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

content:
Abstract

This article presents the results of a synthetic‑data‑based 6D pose estimation pipeline using Deep Object Pose Estimation (DOPE), trained on Isaac Sim–generated datasets for a custom object (Mustertasse). A 50,000‑image synthetic dataset was created using domain randomization, and the trained model was validated in both simulated and real conditions. The results demonstrate accurate sim‑to‑real transfer, supporting the validity of the digital twin as a perception-test environment.

1. Introduction

Reliable 6D pose estimation is essential for robotic manipulation in industrial settings. Synthetic data generated in a digital twin allows scalable training of detection and pose estimation models without costly manual labeling. This study evaluates the DOPE model trained exclusively on Isaac‑Sim‑generated data and assesses its performance across simulated and physical environments.

2. Synthetic Data Generation

A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and exported into Isaac Sim as a USD asset. Using Structured Domain Randomization (SDG), 50,000 images were produced:

  • 20,000 images without distractors
  • 30,000 images with distractor objects

Rendered images include diverse object positions, lighting, distractors, and camera noise models, enabling generalization to real-world sensor conditions.

3. DOPE Training

The DOPE network was trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU for 13.74 days, reaching stable convergence by approximately 2,000 epochs. Training was performed exclusively on synthetic Isaac Sim data, which allowed precise 6D labels without manual annotation.

4. Results

4.1 DOPE Model Performance

The trained model was evaluated in:

  • Isaac Sim (synthetic validation)
  • Real world using an FDM‑printed Mustertasse replica

Results show high visual alignment between predicted and ground truth poses in both conditions, confirming robust sim‑to‑real transfer.

Figure 2 — DOPE Training and Evaluation

CAD model (a), synthetic datasets (b–c), training results (d), inference in simulation (e) and real environment (f).

5. Digital Twin Validation via Perception

The DOPE results support the validity of the digital twin because:

  1. Synthetic images produced in Isaac Sim were sufficiently realistic to train a deployable detector.
  2. The model performed consistently on both the simulated object and the real printed counterpart.
  3. Spatial alignment between real and simulated cameras confirmed accurate calibration.
  4. Sim-to-real transfer of detection and pose estimation demonstrates that the twin has correct geometry, lighting models, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics.

6. Discussion

The findings show that combining Isaac Sim with domain randomization enables large-scale, perfectly labeled datasets for industrial object detection. The strong sim‑to‑real consistency further confirms that digital twins can be used to validate machine‑learning‑based robotics workflows before deploying them on hardware.

7. Conclusion

The DOPE pipeline trained on digital‑twin‑generated data achieved accurate 6D pose estimation in both simulation and real tests. This validates the digital twin as a perception‑testing platform and highlights synthetic data as a scalable strategy for industrial robotics applications.
description: Evaluation of a synthetic-data-driven DOPE pipeline for part detection and pose estimation, and its use in validating a high-fidelity digital twin.
title: Synthetic Data Generation and DOPE-Based Pose Estimation for Industrial Parts Using a Digital Twin

:warning: Note: This digital twin is complete and the platform is being used to develop and test new ideas.

Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.
description: A detailed technical overview of a hybrid physical–simulation robotics platform integrating industrial manipulators, multi-modal sensing, and GPU-accelerated planning.
title: Technical Description of an Industrial Digital Twin Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and ROS 2

content:
Abstract

This article presents the results of a synthetic‑data‑based 6D pose estimation pipeline using Deep Object Pose Estimation (DOPE), trained on Isaac Sim–generated datasets for a custom object (Mustertasse). A 50,000‑image synthetic dataset was created using domain randomization, and the trained model was validated in both simulated and real conditions. The results demonstrate accurate sim‑to‑real transfer, supporting the validity of the digital twin as a perception-test environment.

1. Introduction

Reliable 6D pose estimation is essential for robotic manipulation in industrial settings. Synthetic data generated in a digital twin allows scalable training of detection and pose estimation models without costly manual labeling. This study evaluates the DOPE model trained exclusively on Isaac‑Sim‑generated data and assesses its performance across simulated and physical environments.

2. Synthetic Data Generation

A custom Mustertasse object was modeled in CAD and exported into Isaac Sim as a USD asset. Using Structured Domain Randomization (SDG), 50,000 images were produced:

  • 20,000 images without distractors
  • 30,000 images with distractor objects

Rendered images include diverse object positions, lighting, distractors, and camera noise models, enabling generalization to real-world sensor conditions.

3. DOPE Training

The DOPE network was trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU for 13.74 days, reaching stable convergence by approximately 2,000 epochs. Training was performed exclusively on synthetic Isaac Sim data, which allowed precise 6D labels without manual annotation.

4. Results

4.1 DOPE Model Performance

The trained model was evaluated in:

  • Isaac Sim (synthetic validation)
  • Real world using an FDM‑printed Mustertasse replica

Results show high visual alignment between predicted and ground truth poses in both conditions, confirming robust sim‑to‑real transfer.

5. Digital Twin Validation via Perception

The DOPE results support the validity of the digital twin because:

  1. Synthetic images produced in Isaac Sim were sufficiently realistic to train a deployable detector.
  2. The model performed consistently on both the simulated object and the real printed counterpart.
  3. Spatial alignment between real and simulated cameras confirmed accurate calibration.
  4. Sim-to-real transfer of detection and pose estimation demonstrates that the twin has correct geometry, lighting models, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics.

6. Discussion

The findings show that combining Isaac Sim with domain randomization enables large-scale, perfectly labeled datasets for industrial object detection. The strong sim‑to‑real consistency further confirms that digital twins can be used to validate machine‑learning‑based robotics workflows before deploying them on hardware.

7. Conclusion

The DOPE pipeline trained on digital‑twin‑generated data achieved accurate 6D pose estimation in both simulation and real tests. This validates the digital twin as a perception‑testing platform and highlights synthetic data as a scalable strategy for industrial robotics applications.
description: Evaluation of a synthetic-data-driven DOPE pipeline for part detection and pose estimation, and its use in validating a high-fidelity digital twin.

Abstract

This article presents the technical description of a laboratory‑validated industrial digital twin that integrates physical robotic hardware with a physics‑accurate simulation built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0. The system synchronizes two industrial manipulators, grippers, multi-modal visual sensing, and force-torque data through ROS 2, enabling virtual commissioning, trajectory validation, and perception testing within a unified software and hardware pipeline.

1. Introduction

Digital twins provide a high-fidelity intermediary between simulation and physical robotic systems. The setup described here couples two industrial robots with an Isaac‑Sim‑based virtual environment using ROS 2 middleware, providing a reproducible platform for manipulator control, perception experiments, and GPU‑accelerated path planning.

2. Hardware Configuration

The physical system includes industrial manipulators, adaptive grippers, stereo and wrist‑mounted cameras, teleoperation controllers, and a host workstation.

Table 1 — Hardware Components

Component Description Qty
Industrial robots UR10 (Universal Robots), HC10DT (Yaskawa Motoman), 6‑axis manipulators 2
Grippers Robotiq 2f‑140 and 2f‑85 2
RGB cameras Robotiq wrist cameras 2
Force‑torque sensor Robotiq FT300‑S 1
Stereo cameras Stereolabs ZED 2i 2
Joysticks Teleoperation controllers 2
Compute workstation Ubuntu PC running Isaac Sim and ROS 2 1

3. Software Stack

The system uses:

  • Isaac Sim 5.0 for digital-twin rendering and physics.
  • ROS 2 Humble for hardware abstraction and message passing.
  • MoveIt Servo for teleoperation.
  • cuRobo + Isaac ROS Nvblox for GPU‑accelerated collision-free trajectory generation.
  • YOLO, RF‑DETR, DOPE, FoundationPose for perception and pose estimation.

4. Digital Twin Model

URDF models of robots and grippers are converted into USD assets inside Isaac Sim to achieve high spatial fidelity. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are aligned using hand‑eye calibration, allowing the digital twin to produce synthetic sensor outputs that match real camera views.

5. Methodology

Stage 1 — Data Acquisition

Hardware is connected to ROS 2, with synchronized acquisition of RGB, depth, force‑torque data, and robot joint states. Hand‑eye calibration yields transformations between cameras and the TCP.

Stage 2 — Twin Construction

URDFs are converted to USD; an XRDF description enables cuRobo‑based GPU trajectory generation inside Isaac Sim. Identical ROS namespaces are used for both environments.

Stage 3 — Teleoperation & Validation

MoveIt Servo supports real‑time joystick control. Robot motion and camera images are compared across physical and simulated environments to validate digital twin fidelity.

6. System Performance

Key real‑world performance metrics include:

  • Robot controllers communicate with ROS at ~100 Hz.
  • ZED 2i stereo cameras operate at 1080p @ 30 FPS for RGB–depth generation.
  • Isaac Sim runs at ~30 FPS on workstation hardware.
  • cuRobo + Nvblox enables real‑time collision‑free trajectories even with close‑proximity manipulators.

7. Conclusion

The digital twin infrastructure provides a robust foundation for industrial robotics research, enabling unified experimentation across perception, planning, and teleoperation. The architecture ensures reproducibility, safety, and reduced development time for advanced manipulation tasks.

title: Technical Description of an Industrial Digital Twin Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and ROS 2
